newsitem.title: USA: Traders cheer Fed's changes to open mkt operations.
newsitem.headline: Traders cheer Fed's changes to open mkt operations.

text.p: U.S. Treasury market participants on Thursday gave two thumbs up to changes in the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's open market operations.
But most players said the changes, including moving up the daily intervention time and announcing the size of adds to or drains from the banking system, was long overdue.
"It will have no market impact," said Marc Wanshel, Fed watcher at J.P. Morgan & Co. "The decision to announce sizes is helpful, but I cannot see any reason why they couldn't do it a long time ago."
The New York Fed on Wednesday said it was pushing up its daily open market operation to 1030-1045 EST/1530-1545 GMT from 1130 EST/1630 GMT, effective January 2.

The Fed explained that the repo market was more active earlier in the day, and it would be easier to get its needed collateral at 1030-1045 EST. Soon thereafter, the par amount of the operation will be released.
The New York Fed also said it reserves the right to enter the market more than once a day.

"It is a good fit for everybody. It will give the Fed an earlier indication whether they have done enough," said Richard Tonkin, vice president and head of the financing desk at Zions First National Bank. "At 1130 (EST), if they see Fed funds still tight, they can still correct it and can do a second operation."
Tonkin said that it made no sense for the Fed to continue coming in at 1130 EST. He explained that years ago, dealers needed the extra time to figure out their financing needs.
"With computers, you know immediately where you are as far as your financing needs," Tonkin said. "I wish they would come in even earlier. I would think 0930 or 1000 (EST) would be an ideal time."
Analysts noted that by entering the market early, the New York Fed saves dealers on daylight overdraft charges and also relieves dealers of the need to hold collateral until 1130 EST.
The Fed had been experimenting with early operations for a couple of months, mostly when fed funds were well above target.
On Wednesday the Fed also said it would conduct bill and coupon passes over a period of weeks -- not days -- which received a lukewarm reception from analysts.
"It now adds more uncertainty about what the Fed may come in and buy," said James Blumenthal, money market economist at MCM MoneyWatch.

Wanshel added that doing coupon passes over a number of weeks will create unneeded market volatility. "There will be less predictable tranches and more likely the market gets caught unaware when they do it. When it actually happens, it could (significantly) move the market."
But Wanshel praised the Fed for becoming more transparent with open market operations.
"There is no reason not to," he said. "There is no (monetary) policy content" in open market operations.
He noted that he was surprised that the Fed admitted that it was actually targeting the fed funds rate and not just reserve conditions in shifting to earlier operations.
